title: Henry IV at Canossa
text:
In 1076 the struggle between the young German king Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops came to a head. Henry and his bishops declared the pope deposed. Gregory answered by excommunicating Henry and releasing his subjects from their oaths of loyalty.

The German princes, many of whom resented Henry, seized their chance. They declared that if he was not freed from excommunication within a year he would lose his throne, and they invited the pope to come to Germany early in 1077 to judge the matter. A meeting between the pope and the rebellious princes would almost certainly have ended Henry's reign.

Henry moved first. In midwinter he crossed the Alps with his wife, his young son and a small following and went to meet the pope, who had stopped at the castle of Canossa in northern Italy, the fortress of Countess Matilda of Tuscany. According to the chronicler Lampert of Hersfeld and Gregory's own letter, Henry stood outside the castle gate as a penitent, barefoot and in woolen clothes, for three days in January 1077, asking for forgiveness. As a priest, Gregory could hardly refuse a penitent, and after three days he absolved him.

The humiliation became legendary, but it achieved its purpose: the princes lost their main argument. They elected a rival king anyway, but Henry fought a civil war and survived. In 1084 he took Rome, and Gregory died in exile the next year.
lesson: Sometimes the strongest move is to give your opponent what he cannot refuse. A public act of humility can disarm a coalition that was waiting to judge you.
people: Henry IV, Pope Gregory VII, Matilda of Tuscany
source: Gregory VII, letter to the German princes (1077); Lampert of Hersfeld, Annals
caveat: Lampert's vivid details of Henry's suffering in the snow may be exaggerated.
